## Ezekiel 39 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

- Ezekiel 39 continues and expands upon chapter 38. It is common in Hebrew literature to give an account and then retell it with greater emphasis and detail. Chapter 38 concentrates on the threat; chapter 39 concentrates on the deliverance and the aftermath. (enduringword.com)
- The Pulpit Commentary divides the chapter: vv. 1–20 depict the greatness of Gog's overthrow; vv. 21–29 record the impression made on Israel and the nations, plus a closing promise. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- Ellicott sees the prophecy as setting forth under the figure of Gog *all opposition of the world to the kingdom of God*, foretelling the final triumph of God's kingdom — not confined to any single literal event. (studylight.org, Ellicott)

---

### vv. 1–2 — Yahweh Directs Gog to Attack

**v. 1:** "As for you, O son of man, prophesy against Gog… I am against you, O Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal."

- This repeats Ezekiel 38:1–2. The repetition is for emphasis; Ezekiel 39:1–8 summarises what was described in chapter 38. (enduringword.com)
- Gill notes that "I am against thee" is repeated to inject terror — terrible it is to have God against any. Gog is identified as the administrative civil ruler of Meshech and Tubal. (biblehub.com, Gill)
- Precept Austin: "Behold" is an interjection demanding attention; the essence of Ezekiel's message is that God is opposed to Gog. (preceptaustin.org)

**v. 2:** "I will turn you around, drive you along, bring you up from the far north, and send you against the mountains of Israel."

- God sovereignly directs Gog. Though Gog comes of his own evil volition (38:10), God "turns" and "leads" him. (enduringword.com)
- The KJV reads "leave but the sixth part of thee," suggesting only 1/6 survive. The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew is disputed: some derive it from the numeral six, others from a root meaning "to lead on." Modern translations lack any quantification. Precept Austin notes scholars are not agreed; v. 4 says 100% fall. (preceptaustin.org; studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- Gill interprets the "sixth part" as meaning five-sixths of his subjects accompany him, draining his country — not that a sixth survives. (biblehub.com, Gill)

---

### vv. 3–5 — Gog Defeated

**v. 3:** "Then I will strike the bow from your left hand and dash down the arrows from your right hand."

- A skilled archer is rendered helpless when his bow is knocked from his left hand and arrows dropped from his right. Bows and arrows were characteristic weapons of the Scythians (Herodotus). (enduringword.com; studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: God leaves Gog defenceless on the battlefield. (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)

**v. 4:** "On the mountains of Israel you will fall — you and all your troops … I will give you as food to every kind of ravenous bird and wild beast."

- Total defeat: Gog and all his allies die in Israel. Their unburied corpses become food for scavengers — a disgrace and a covenant curse (cf. Deut 28:26). (enduringword.com)
- Gill: This was considered a dreadful calamity among the heathen; Homer and Virgil both mention exposure to birds and dogs as the severest punishment. (biblehub.com, Gill)
- Precept Austin notes the Holman Christian Study Bible links vv. 4–9 to Revelation 19:17–18, perhaps referring to the same event. (preceptaustin.org)

**v. 5:** "You will fall in the open field, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD."

- Some fall on the mountains, others on the plain — wherever found, all destroyed. "For I have spoken" assures the certainty of it. (biblehub.com, Gill)
- Precept Austin: "For it is I Who have spoken" explains why Gog's doom is a done deal. (preceptaustin.org)

---

### vv. 6–8 — Magog Attacked; God's Name Glorified

**v. 6:** "I will send fire on Magog and on those who dwell securely in the coastlands, and they will know that I am the LORD."

- Not only the invading forces but their homeland (Magog) is devastated by divine fire. "Fire" is a common expression for divine judgment (Hos 8:14; Amos 1:12). (preceptaustin.org)
- Gill: While Gog perishes in Israel, his country is destroyed by fire — the destruction of the Ottoman empire is in view for Gill. (biblehub.com, Gill)
- EnduringWord: "Coastlands" refers to unspecified distant coastlands or islands, not a distinct nation. Some speculate about the United States, but there is no textual foundation for this. (enduringword.com)
- Precept Austin quotes Joel Rosenberg: parts of Russia and other enemy countries devastated by fire from heaven — supernatural, not Israeli defence forces. (preceptaustin.org)

**v. 7:** "So I will make My holy name known among My people Israel and will no longer allow it to be profaned."

- God's supernatural defence of Israel will demonstrate His holiness to His own people and stop the profaning of His name. (preceptaustin.org)
- Precept Austin argues that "no longer…profaned anymore" points to the end of this age: only after this age will God's name not be profaned anymore. If the Gog battle occurred before the Tribulation, this statement would be invalid, since God's name is clearly blasphemed during the Great Tribulation. (preceptaustin.org)
- Gill: Either the heathen will stop blaspheming, or Israel will be so influenced by grace that they will not commit the sins that caused God's name to be profaned. (biblehub.com, Gill)

**v. 8:** "Yes, it is coming, and it will surely happen … This is the day of which I have spoken."

- God solemnly affirms the prophecy. The Pulpit Commentary calls this a bold anthropomorphism — words a man might speak on seeing his purpose accomplished, put into the mouth of Jehovah. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- Garner-Howes: The irrevocable purpose of God was so fixed and certain it is spoken as if already accomplished (cf. Rom 4:17). (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)

---

### vv. 9–10 — Defeated Gog Plundered by Israel

**v. 9:** "Then those who dwell in the cities of Israel will go out, kindle fires, and burn up the weapons … For seven years they will use them for fuel."

- The vast quantity of weapons left by Gog's armies is so immense that Israel will burn them for fuel for seven years. (enduringword.com)
- The weapons listed — bucklers, shields, bows, arrows, clubs, spears — are not modern; Ezekiel used language his audience understood. (enduringword.com, citing Wiersbe)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that most of these weapons were composed of timber, hence combustible. The burning also indicates that in the Messianic age such weapons will no longer be needed (cf. Isa 2:4). The "seven years" is symbolic — seven being the number of completion. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- Precept Austin: "Seven years" can be taken literally; the number of weapons defies imagination, indicating a vast army. If this battle corresponds to Revelation 19:19–21, the burning could extend into the Millennium. (preceptaustin.org)

**v. 10:** "They will not gather wood from the countryside … They will loot those who looted them and plunder those who plundered them."

- So much fuel from weapons that no wood needs to be gathered from field or forest. The *lex talionis* (law of retaliation) is at work: the plunderers become the plundered. (enduringword.com; studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- Garner-Howes: They are directed to spoil those who came to spoil them — by the Lord who owns the earth and all things in it. (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)

---

### vv. 11–16 — Defeated Gog Buried by Israel

**v. 11:** "I will give Gog a burial place in Israel, the Valley of the Travelers, east of the Sea … Valley of Hamon-gog."

- Gog, who hoped to possess the whole land, receives only a grave in it. The burial is more about cleansing the land than honouring the dead; unburied bodies defile the land (Num 19:11–22). (enduringword.com)
- The location is disputed. The Pulpit Commentary summarises: some say the valley near the Dead Sea; others the valley of Megiddo (where Josiah fell); still others argue for a location near the Sea of Galilee. The phrase "east of the sea" on the Megiddo view would mean east of the Mediterranean, which is too vague. The Dead Sea view is preferred by Keil, Havernick, and others. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- Gill: "It shall stop the noses of the passengers" — the stench from the multitude of corpses will be so great that passers-by will hold their noses. (biblehub.com, Gill)
- Hamon-gog means "the multitude of Gog." (enduringword.com)

**v. 12:** "For seven months the house of Israel will be burying them in order to cleanse the land."

- The burial effort takes seven months — indicating the staggering number of slain. Precept Austin: even if one person buried two bodies a day, the total would be in the millions. (preceptaustin.org)
- The purpose is to cleanse the land — not merely ceremonial (since ceremonial law will be abrogated when Jews are converted), but from natural pollution and disease. (biblehub.com, Gill)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the sacred number seven recalls the seven years of burning weapons. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)

**v. 13:** "All the people of the land will bury them, and it will bring them renown on the day I display My glory."

- The whole population participates. The work brings them renown ("a name"), not because they helped defeat Gog, but because in the day God glorifies Himself, they are honoured to share in cleansing the land. (biblehub.com, Gill; studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- The KJV Bible Commentary (cited at Precept Austin): "This gruesome task would appear to have a very sobering influence spiritually. No doubt it will prove to be one of the means of leading Israel, as well as the Gentiles, to repentance and faith in the Lord." (preceptaustin.org)

**v. 14:** "And men will be employed to continually pass through the land to cleanse it … At the end of the seven months they will begin their search."

- After the seven months of mass burial, a special corps of "men of continual employment" is appointed to conduct a thorough search for remaining bones. The Pulpit Commentary details a debated question: whether there were two classes — "searchers" and "buriers" — or one body doing both. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- The work is organised and thorough; nothing is left to chance. (enduringword.com)

**v. 15:** "Anyone who sees a human bone will set up a pillar next to it, until the gravediggers have buried it in the Valley of Hamon-gog."

- A marker (a stone or heap of stones) is erected by any passer-by who spots a bone, so that the official burial teams can locate and inter it. (biblehub.com, Gill)
- Precept Austin: after several days, flesh decays and predators scatter bones, leaving only skeletons to be found. (preceptaustin.org)

**v. 16:** " (Even the city will be named Hamonah.) And so they will cleanse the land."

- Hamonah means "Multitude." The city may be a new settlement near the burial site, or a headquarters for the burial operation. The LXX translates it *Polyandrion*, a term for a common cemetery. (enduringword.com, citing Wiersbe; studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- Gill observes that no city in Israel has ever borne this name, which suggests the prophecy is yet future. (biblehub.com, Gill)

---

### vv. 17–20 — The Grotesque Sacrificial Feast

**v. 17:** "Call out to every kind of bird and to every beast of the field: 'Assemble and come … to the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you …'"

- The scene is a grim reversal: instead of humans consuming sacrificial animals, animals consume human "sacrifices." God invites birds and beasts to feast on the corpses of His defeated enemies. (enduringword.com)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes Ezekiel borrows imagery from Isaiah (34:6; 56:9) and Jeremiah (46:10). (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- Precept Austin: carnivorous birds and beasts consume the flesh of the fallen. (preceptaustin.org)

**v. 18:** "You will eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth as though they were rams, lambs, goats, and bulls — all the fattened animals of Bashan."

- The mighty men and princes are described in sacrificial animal terms — rams, lambs, goats, bulls, fatlings of Bashan (Bashan was known for its rich pasture and fat livestock; cf. Ps 22:12). This is God's "sacrifice." (enduringword.com; studyylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: these unclean fowls and beasts are filled with dead flesh of men and horses — mighty men of politics, commerce, and war. (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)

**v. 19:** "At the sacrifice I am preparing, you will eat fat until you are gorged and drink blood until you are drunk."

- The grotesque hyperbole conveys the sheer scale of carnage — so many corpses that scavengers cannot consume them all. (enduringword.com)

**v. 20:** "And at My table you will eat your fill of horses and riders, of mighty men and warriors of every kind."

- "My table" is the Lord's sacrificial table — a vivid figure of vast carnage, deserved judgment, and irrevocable doom. (enduringword.com, citing Feinberg)
- **Connection to Revelation:** EnduringWord notes that John links this feast to the battle of Armageddon (Rev 19:17–21) and also links the Gog invasion to a battle at the end of the Millennium (Rev 20:7–9). Because John links aspects of Ezekiel 38–39 to *two chronologically separated events*, it is likely he uses Ezekiel 38–39 as *examples* rather than the events actually fulfilling the prophecies. (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 21–24 — God Vindicated Among the Nations

**v. 21:** "I will display My glory among the nations, and all the nations will see the judgment that I execute and the hand that I lay upon them."

- God's glory is set among the nations through His judgment on Gog. Precept Austin: "Glory" (*kabod*) speaks of weightiness; God will give the nations a proper opinion of His character. (preceptaustin.org)
- The Pulpit Commentary: this section records the impression Gog's overthrow makes on Israel and the heathen. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)

**v. 22:** "From that day forward the house of Israel will know that I am the LORD their God."

- This points to a permanent turning point in Israel's relationship with God. Precept Austin: God's Spirit opens Israel's heart to see, know, and love the LORD as their personal God — this happens when they repent and believe in their Messiah (cf. Rom 11:26–27). (preceptaustin.org)
- Garner-Howes: Israel shall recognise from that day and forever that the Lord is God. (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)

**v. 23:** "And the nations will know that the house of Israel went into exile for their iniquity, because they were unfaithful to Me."

- The nations will understand that Israel's suffering was not due to Yahweh's weakness but to Israel's sin. God hid His face because of their unfaithfulness. (enduringword.com, citing Poole: "The sottish heathen thought meanly of the God of Israel… but by this overthrow given to Gog, they shall see it was not impotence in Israel's God, but iniquity in Israel's people.")
- The Pulpit Commentary: The special lesson for the heathen is not about God's supremacy but about the *principles* of God's dealings with Israel. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)

**v. 24:** "I dealt with them according to their uncleanness and transgressions, and I hid My face from them."

- Garner-Howes: It was solely because of their uncleanness and transgressions that He gave them over to the consequences of their chosen ways. (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)
- The phrase "hid My face" occurs in Ezekiel only here and v. 29, though it is common in the Pentateuch and older prophets. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)

---

### vv. 25–29 — God in Fellowship with His Restored People

**v. 25:** "Now I will restore Jacob from captivity and will have compassion on the whole house of Israel, and I will be jealous for My holy name."

- Hengstenberg regards vv. 25–29 as the close of the entire series of consolatory prophecies from Ezekiel 33:21 onward. The prophet shifts from the distant future (Gog) back to the nearer future (return from exile), because that was of immediate interest to the exiles. (studylight.org, Hengstenberg)
- Garner-Howes: partial restorations have occurred, but a universal one is yet to come (Jer 30:3; Rom 11:26; Hos 1:11). (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)
- EnduringWord: Ezekiel first spoke these words to Babylonian exiles; they had a minor, imperfect fulfilment under Ezra and Zerubbabel; the greater fulfilment still waits (Rom 11:26). (enduringword.com)

**v. 26:** "They will forget their disgrace and all the treachery they committed against Me, when they dwell securely in their land, with no one to frighten them."

- Israel's restoration comes in a spirit of deep repentance. They bear their shame even as they dwell securely, and this attitude of repentance sanctifies God in the sight of the nations. (enduringword.com, citing Morgan and Block)
- The Pulpit Commentary: the captivity will not be brought back until the people have been thoroughly chastised and chastisement has wrought penitence. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)

**v. 27:** "When I bring them back from the peoples and gather them out of the lands of their enemies, I will show My holiness in them in the sight of many nations."

- God's holy name is vindicated in His dealing with His people — both in exiling them for sin and in restoring them by grace. (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)
- Whedon's Commentary: When the new Israel is brought back, filled with shame for past sins and joy in God's presence, Jehovah is sanctified in them. (studylight.org, Whedon)

**v. 28:** "Then they will know that I am the LORD their God, when I regather them to their own land, not leaving any of them behind after their exile among the nations."

- EnduringWord (citing Block): Ezekiel's declaration that not a single individual will be left behind is "without parallel in the OT." Yahweh's restoration is total and permanent. (enduringword.com)

**v. 29:** "And I will no longer hide My face from them, for I will pour out My Spirit on the house of Israel."

- The ultimate blessing: God's Spirit poured out, ensuring a permanent relationship. EnduringWord notes the Hebrew uses the "prophetic perfect" tense — "I *have* poured out My Spirit" — speaking of the future as if already accomplished, so certain is the promise. (enduringword.com, citing Taylor)
- The Pulpit Commentary connects this to Joel 2:28 and Peter's citation at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). Peter saw the Pentecost outpouring as a fulfilment, yet the promise was not exhausted then; it will receive its consummation in the New Jerusalem. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- Gill: After this, God will no more hide His face; His Spirit's influence ensures they will ever continue in obedience. (biblehub.com, Gill)
- Precept Austin ties this to Isa 32:15, 44:3–5, 59:20–21, and Joel 2:28. (preceptaustin.org)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Based on what I could retrieve, the key differences among Protestant traditions on Ezekiel 39 centre on **timing and literalism**, not so much on individual verses:

### Dispensational / Premillennial (common in many Baptist and Pentecostal circles)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary takes a strongly literal, futurist approach: Gog is a real future ruler, the weapons are literal, the seven years and seven months are literal time spans, and the battle is yet future — connected to Armageddon (Rev 19) and to the conversion of national Israel. (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)
- Precept Austin quotes John MacArthur (a prominent dispensational Baptist): the scene adds detail to Ezekiel 38:18–23, and if the battle corresponds to Revelation 16:16 and 19:19–21, the burning of weapons extends into the Millennium. (preceptaustin.org)
- Precept Austin itself leans futurist: Israel's rebirth (1948) is a partial fulfilment; Ezekiel 38–39 events occur between that rebirth and the Millennium (Ezek 40–48). (preceptaustin.org)
- *I was unable to retrieve specific pages from gty.org, desiringgod.org, or spurgeon.org.*

### Reformed / Amillennial or Postmillennial
- Ellicott argues the prophecy is *not confined to any literal event* but sets forth under the figure of Gog *all opposition of the world to the kingdom of God*, foretelling the final triumph of the latter. This is a classic amillennial/spiritual reading. (studylight.org, Ellicott)
- The Pulpit Commentary, while not denying a future conflict, says the whole delineation is *symbolic* and embodies spiritual truths under material emblems — citing Fairbairn's arguments that a literal invasion of Israel with literal weapons is improbable given the symbolic nature of the numbers, weapons, and geography. (studylight.org, Pulpit Commentary)
- *I was unable to retrieve specific pages from ligonier.org, monergism.com, or thegospelcoalition.org.*

### Lutheran
- Hengstenberg (Lutheran/Reformed): The dogmatic idea is that "the community of God, renewed by His grace, will victoriously resist all the assaults of the world." The prophecy unites in one grand picture what is realised over a long series of successive events. Applications to a single historical event are "at the same time true and false." (studylight.org, Hengstenberg)
- *I was unable to retrieve pages from lcms.org or 1517.org.*

### Methodist / Wesleyan
- Whedon's Commentary (Methodist): The promise is to be "fulfilled truly, though not literally." It has received partial fulfilment (cf. Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17), yet Gog "has certainly not yet been left dead upon the field." The final fulfilment may be on earth or only in the heavenly city. (studylight.org, Whedon)
- *I was unable to retrieve pages from seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu.*

### Anglican
- Ellicott (Anglican): The prophecy may have partial fulfilments (Scythian invasion, Maccabean conflict with Antiochus) but its ultimate reference is the final struggle and triumph of God's kingdom. (studylight.org, Ellicott)

## Summary of Key Interpretive Questions Not Fully Resolved

1. **Identity of Gog/Magog:** Literal future ruler from the north vs. symbolic representation of all anti-God world powers.
2. **Timing:** Before the Tribulation, at Armageddon (end of Tribulation), or at the end of the Millennium (cf. Rev 20:7–9). EnduringWord notes Revelation uses Ezekiel 38–39 motifs for *both* Armageddon and the post-Millennial battle, suggesting John uses Ezekiel typologically rather than as direct fulfilment.
3. **Literal vs. Symbolic:** The weapons (bows, arrows, shields, clubs), the "seven years" of burning, the "seven months" of burial — are these literal or symbolic of completeness?
4. **Israel:** Is the restoration in vv. 25–29 fulfilled in the return from Babylon, in the Church, or in a future national conversion of ethnic Israel (Rom 11:26)?
5. **The Spirit outpouring (v. 29):** Fulfilled at Pentecost (Pulpit, Whedon) vs. awaiting a future eschatological outpouring on national Israel (Garner-Howes, Precept Austin).
